meta.description: Building 109 supports multiple functions within the 194th Logistics Readiness Squadron, including LGRM, LGRDX, LGLO, LGRDDO and the Command Section. Personnel assigned to the facility perform a variety of logistics, administrative, supply, transportation, and mission support duties in support of the 194th Wing. This JSTO establishes the required safety training for personnel assigned to Bldg. 109 and addresses common workplace hazards, emergency procedures, PPE requirements, mishap prevention, and safe work practices. Personnel will also comply with work-center specific JHA's, operating procedures, and safety requirements applicable to their assigned duties.

meta.jhaNotes:
HAZARDS OF THE JOB	SPECIFIC PRECAUTIONS/REQUIREMENTS

	Material Handling:	Always lift with your legs, not your back.  Squat down, grasp the item close to your body, and lift straight up.  Do not twist your body to turn.  If you need to turn, pivot on your heels in the direction you need to turn.  Avoid any necessary twisting and lower the item in the same way you lift it. If you need help lifting an object because it is too heave or awkward ask for assistance. 

	Walking/Working Surfaces:	Walk, don’t run.  Be aware of items (cords, loose carpet, pencils, paper, etc.) that may cause you to slip/trip and fall.  Climb stairs facing forward, stay to the right side, use the handrail and avoid distractions that may cause you to fall.  Do not run up or down stairs.

	Stairwell Safety:	Do not run up or down stairs, always use hand rails.  Do not skip steps if in a hurry.  If carrying packages be sure of your footing. When climbing stairs stay to your right.  When going down stairs stay to your right. Report any damage to stairs or hand rail to your building custodian.

	Electrical Hazards: Computers and other electrically powered equipment are used in the office environment.  Ensure all electrically operated equipment has a ground prong, if manufactured with one, and that all prongs are securely attached.  When plugging and unplugging electrical equipment, grasp the base of the cord.  Frequently inspect cords for damage.  If you feel a shock or tingling sensation when touching a piece of equipment, turn it off at the power strip or circuit breaker and notify your supervisor.  Multiple plug adapters will not be used solely as wiring to provide additional or more convenient outlets. Power strips should only support low wattage equipment. Do not plug coffee makers, microwaves, refrigerators, etc. into these.  In addition, do not plug any higher amperage devices into modular furniture (microwaves, toasters, refrigerators), as the wiring inside is not designed to carry these loads and a fire may result.

	Hand Tool Safety: You may occasionally be required to use tools in the office (utility knives, screw drivers, etc.).  Ensure you always cut away from your body.  Do not carry and/or store unguarded blades or sharp objects in your pockets or desk drawers.  There are assortments of hand tools that may be used in an office environment.  Ensure that all tools are used for the purposes for which they were designed.  Inspect tools prior to use.  If an unsafe tool is found, remove it from service and report it to your supervisor.

	Repetitive Motion Hazards:  Repetitive tasks such as typing may create problems for some individuals.  To avoid such problems, alternate tasks to prevent the over-exertion of a particular body part or series of parts.  Your supervisor should provide you with the latitude to alternate tasks without hindering mission effectiveness.  Schedule your daily tasks with this in mind.

	Office Safety:	Desks, tables and many other pieces of office furniture have sharp corners that can cause injury.  Use caution particularly when walking around desks.  Open file cabinet drawers one at a time to prevent possible tipping.  Desk and cabinet drawers should never be left unattended in the open position.  Position office equipment in a manner that egress and ease of movement is not hampered.  Proper sitting is important.  Employees leaning back or sitting on the front edge of the seat creates mishaps/falls from chairs.
meta.medicalFacility:
LOCATION OF MEDICAL FACILITIES & PROCEDURES FOR OBTAINING TREATMENT

	Emergency Medical Treatment is not avalible on Camp Murray. 

	The nearest Emergency Medical Facility is located on JBLM at the Madigan Army Medical Center. 
 
	Madigan Army Medical Center is located on Lewis Main and is on Jackson Ave.  The emergency room is located on the north side of the building.  All active duty military personnel, whether full-time or part-time, are authorized to use the hospital for emergency treatment.

	For non-emergencies, appointments must be made at McChord  medical appointment line, phone number: 1-800-404-4506.  Dental services are also available at McChord by calling 982-5505.   Call 911 for emergencies. 

	Air Force and DoD civilian personnel must complete a Form CA-1 or CA-6 (obtained from supervisor/safety representative).  This should be completed as soon as possible after medical treatment is sought.  Contact the civilian personnel office for assistance, 253-512-7944.

	If emergency responders are needed, call 911 from any base telephone. (Note: If you dial 911 from your cell phone, it may delay response since the call goes to an off-base responder). The Fire Department will respond with paramedics/EMTs that are on shift. They can evaluate the injuries and recommend further medical attention. If further medical attention is needed, an ambulance may be called to transport the individual to a medical facility. If it is not a severe injury, but the person feels that a doctor needs to check it, they may go to an off-base medical provider of their choice within a reasonable distance (25 miles).

meta.activeShooterMethods:
Active shooter response methods: AVOID, DENY, DEFEND: After being notified of an active shooter (At Hoc, GIANT VOICE, radio network, landline telephone, cellphone, gunfire, etc.), unit members should do one of the following if able to, and not necessarily in this order. Members should always consider what method provides them the best chance for survival:

a. Avoid: Avoid is a state of mind and it is not always the physical action of moving away (run) from danger and drives more to be constantly aware of your surroundings. Get out if you can, even if others insist on staying. Consider all points of egress as potential escape routes (e.g., windows, doors). Leave belongings behind. Your life is more precious than "things". Move tactically (e.g., stay low, move quickly and silently our of harms way). Once out, seek shelter far away from the ASI and call 9- 1-1. Be prepared to provide as much information as possible (5W's- Who, What, When, Where and Why-if known). If wounded are encountered during escape evacuation, do not treat the wounded in the danger area-assist in their escape (if possible) and only treat wounded when properly barricaded.

b. Deny: Deny the attacker access to you and those around you. Hiding is an option but has proven problematic during ASIs. The idea of "hide and hope" is not an effective survival strategy during an ASI. If you can't get out, find a place of cover and concealment. Barricade or lock doors. Take cover behind large/solid objects. Turn out lights and silence your phone / radios and remain quiet. Do not report your location or who is with you via social media.

c. Defend: It is important to be prepared to fight for your life. The word defend emphasizes your legal right to defend yourself and others in harm’s way, which includes protecting, resisting, and fighting for your life. Attempt to incapacitate the shooter. Act with overwhelming aggression and maximum violence. Improvise weapons and throw objects at the shooter. Commit to your actions.

meta.trafficSafetyNotes:
	MANDATORY USE OF SEAT BELTS:  AFI 91-207, The US Air Force Traffic Safety Program, outlines the requirements for seat belt use.  Safety belts will be worn by anyone driving or riding in a vehicle on base.  Active duty personnel must wear safety belts when operating a vehicle (regardless whether it is a GOV or POV) on or off base.  AF civilian personnel on duty must wear seat belts on or off a DoD installation.    Children 1.50 meters (4 ft, 9 inches) in height or smaller regardless of age must be in an infant seat or child restraint device. As a vehicle operator, you are responsible for ensuring all passengers are using safety belts.  Traffic violations for passengers not wearing safety belts go to the operator.

NOTE:  Placing the shoulder strap under the arm or not using/disconnecting automatic belts constitutes improper use and may result in a citation or more seriously, death or disability.

	IAW DODI 6055.4 (Traffic Safety Program) and AFI 91-207, The US Air Force Traffic Safety Program, the use of headphones, earphones, and cellular telephones is prohibited while operating a vehicle on a DoD installation.  The only caveat to this is using a hands free device or in hands-free operating mode.  

	SPEED LIMITS:
•	You, as a driver, have to follow speed limits on and off base.
•	On base the general speed limit is 25 mph if no other sign is posted.
•	The basic speed limit off base is 35 mph in built-up areas and 55 mph on roadways.  Typically, on highways, it is 60 mph.  If you are hauling a trailer, camper, or boat, reduce your speed to prevent from tipping over or jackknifing.

	LOCAL TRAFFIC HAZARDS:
•	DRIVING DURING WINTER in this area is extremely dangerous with ice and snow because the roads are over populated and there are numerous curves and hills.  Black ice can increase risk of accidents, so slow down and take your time during the winter months.  We would rather have you arrive a few minutes late, than not at all!

•	HIGHWAY I-5:  You may or may not have heard of the motor vehicle mishaps on the I-5; however, according to the Air Force Safety Center, the Air Force loses roughly on average 18 Airmen annually due to fatal motor vehicle mishaps.  Protect yourself by reducing your speed and driving defensively.  This means expect other drivers to speed and pass at the worst times, and adjust your driving to avoid an accident.

•	RURAL ROADS:  Here in Washington, we have roadways 7, 8, 12, 101, 121, 161, 162, 167, 410, 507, 510, 512, and 706.  These roadways on average have a maximum speed limit of 35 mph to 60 mph.  These roadways can also become congested with traffic and occasional farm equipment.  If you are stuck behind a piece of farm equipment, do not try passing unless it is safe and legal to do so.  Be sure to plan ahead so you do not need to rush.  Lastly, during the wintertime, these roads are secondary when it comes to sanding and plowing.  It is important to know this in case you need to make other arrangements when it comes to getting to your destination.  The most serious accidents occur when people drive faster than the road conditions will safely allow.  Use common sense and reduce your speed for poor weather conditions and congested traffic.
meta.trafficContacts: •	MOTORCYCLE RIDERS: Motorcycle riders must have a motorcycle endorsement from a state, and have attended a Motorcycle Safety Foundation (Basic Rider or Basic rider II Course).  Additionally, each rider must make contact with their unit Motorcycle Safety Representative (MSR).  The rider must receive a unit safety briefing from their MSR or designated representative before riding.  All riders must also complete an MSF-approved intermediate training course (sport bike riders must take a sport bike riding course) ideally within 60 days but no later than one year after completing initial training. See AFI 91-207.  Annual preseason briefings are also required.
